segments.text: Part 3. You will hear two marine biology students discussing their tutor's comments on a field report they wrote together. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

part.title: Feedback on a field report

turns.text: Hi Liam. Have you had a chance to look at Dr Sutherland's feedback on our field report?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, I read it on the bus this morning. It's better than I expected, actually. We got a credit, and she reckons we could get a distinction if we fix a few things in the final version.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Oh, that's a relief. I was sure she'd rave about the photos, given how long we spent taking them on the rock platform at Long Reef.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: She mentioned them, but only in passing. And the introduction got a tick, but nothing more. What she really praised was the way we explained how we laid out the quadrats and counted everything. She said another student could repeat our survey exactly, just from reading that section.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's great, because I rewrote that bit about three times. So what about the results? I thought that section was pretty solid.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Mostly, yes. I thought she might complain that we'd shown the same data in a table and a graph, but she was fine with that. The problem is the bar charts. We left the units off the axes, so the reader can't tell if we mean snails per quadrat or per square metre.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Oh no. Well, at least that's quick to fix. Did she say anything about the captions?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: She said they were clear, so we can leave those alone.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good. And the discussion? I was a bit worried it went on too long.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: No, she said the length was about right. And she was happy with the sources, too. Eight journal articles is plenty at this level. The real issue is that we never actually say whether our hypothesis was supported. We set it up in the introduction, that there'd be more snails closer to the low-water mark, and then we never come back to it.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right, so we need a paragraph that answers it directly. Yes or no, and why.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Exactly. Then there's the species list in the appendix. She questioned whether it should be there at all.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Well, I don't want to delete it. It took us ages to put together. Could we add a photo of each species to make it more useful?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That'd double the length of the report. Her suggestion was to turn it into a table in the results, because really it's part of our data, not extra information.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Yeah, that makes sense. Let's do that. Anything else?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Just the site map. She said the scale bar and north arrow were fine, and she was pleased it was our own drawing, not copied from somewhere. But it doesn't show where our three transects actually ran, so the reader can't link the results to particular spots on the platform.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: OK, so for the final version, how about you redo the map, since you're better at that sort of thing?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Sure. I was going to take a screenshot from Google Maps, but there might be copyright issues. So I'll base it on aerial photographs from the New South Wales government website. They're free to use.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Perfect. Oh, and I noticed something else she wrote in the margin. We've got the wind speed and the tide height for the survey day, but we didn't include the water temperature, and that affects how active the snails are.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Did we even record that? Oh, yes, it's in my notebook. I'll add it to the methods.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Great. And there's that one periwinkle we weren't sure about. Dr Sutherland's away at a conference until next week, so I'll ask the lab technician to have a look at our photo and confirm what it is.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Good idea. What about the introduction? She said it's too long.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: It's about 550 words at the moment. I think we should get it down to around 300.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I'd have said 250, but that might be too short to explain the hypothesis properly. OK, 300 it is.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: And the referencing. We used APA because that's what we did in first year, but the course guide says it has to be Harvard style.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Oh, really? I'll go through and change them. It won't take long.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: So when should we put it all together? We could meet at your flat.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: It's a bit far for you, isn't it? Why don't we book a room in the science library? They've got big screens, so we can both edit at once.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good thinking. And the deadline's the 7th of October, isn't it?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: It was, but they've extended it for everyone because the field trip was postponed. It's now due on Friday, 14 October.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Great, that gives us a bit of breathing space. Let's aim to finish a few days early, though.
turns.speaker: student_a
